mcqs.question: What makes a comment box vulnerable to XSS when it renders a stored `<script>` tag back to visitors?
options: The browser parses the stored string as HTML and executes the script tag, since untrusted data and executable markup share one channel with no separation
The database failed to encrypt the comment before storing it
The comment exceeded the server's maximum input length
The server used an outdated TLS version for the response
mcqs.explanation: The browser has no way to distinguish a developer's intended HTML from attacker-supplied HTML once they're rendered in the same unescaped channel, so a `<script>` tag gets parsed and executed just like any other markup. Encryption, input length, and TLS version are unrelated to whether the browser treats the string as code.

mcqs.question: Why is stored XSS generally considered more severe than reflected XSS?
options: It requires the victim to click a specially crafted link
It only affects the attacker's own account
The payload persists server-side and executes for every subsequent visitor, including admins, with no phishing click required
It can only be triggered through URL parameters
mcqs.explanation: Because the payload is saved and served to everyone who views that content, stored XSS reaches a much larger and more privileged audience — including moderators or admins — without needing a victim to click anything. Reflected XSS, not stored, is the one that requires a crafted link and URL parameters.

mcqs.question: A page reads `location.hash` and writes it directly into `innerHTML` client-side. Why might a server-side security review completely miss this vulnerability?
options: Because URL fragments are always blocked by modern browsers
Because DOM-based XSS can only be exploited by the site's own developers
Because the payload never reaches the server at all — the URL fragment isn't sent by default, so the bug lives entirely in client-side JavaScript
Because server logs always redact URL fragments automatically
mcqs.explanation: The URL fragment after `#` isn't transmitted to the server by default, so a server-side code or log review has nothing to inspect — the vulnerable code path is purely client-side JavaScript writing into a sink like `innerHTML`. Fragments aren't blocked by browsers, this isn't restricted to internal developers, and log redaction isn't the mechanism.

mcqs.question: A developer HTML-encodes user input before inserting it into a `<script>var name = "{data}";</script>` block. Why doesn't this fully protect against XSS?
options: HTML encoding is unnecessary in script contexts and can be skipped entirely
Script tags are never parsed by browsers if they contain any encoded entities
This is actually sufficient protection for any context the data is inserted into
HTML entity encoding doesn't neutralize the characters that break out of a JavaScript string, so a value like `";alert(1);//` can still execute
mcqs.explanation: Each rendering context — HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL — has its own escape characters, and HTML encoding only covers the HTML-body case; a JavaScript string needs JavaScript-specific encoding to stop a quote from ending the string early. It's not that encoding is unnecessary or universally sufficient — using the wrong encoding for the context is exactly the trap.

mcqs.question: A site sets `Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self'` but still has an unescaped output-encoding bug that lets an attacker inject `<script>...</script>` into a page. What happens?
options: The injected script still executes normally, since CSP only affects network requests
CSP automatically detects and removes the injected script tag from the page
The page fails to load entirely because CSP blocks all scripts, including the site's own
The browser refuses to execute the injected inline script because it isn't from an allowed source, limiting the damage even though the underlying bug remains
mcqs.explanation: A strict `script-src` policy rejects inline scripts and scripts from other origins, so the browser won't run the injected payload even though the encoding bug let it into the page — that's CSP acting as a backstop, not a fix for the underlying bug. It doesn't block the site's own legitimate same-origin scripts, doesn't remove tags, and does affect script execution, not just network requests.

mcqs.question: A team blocks any input containing the literal string `<script>` to prevent XSS. Why is this insufficient?
options: Because `<script>` tags are already blocked by all modern browsers regardless of server behavior
Because vectors like `` or a `javascript:` URL execute script without ever containing the word "script", and case or encoding variants bypass a literal match
Because blocking `<script>` breaks all legitimate HTML rendering on the page
Because XSS can only occur through form submissions, not through blocked strings
mcqs.explanation: A blocklist checks for known-bad patterns, but plenty of execution vectors — event handler attributes, SVG payloads, javascript: URLs — never use the word "script" at all, and simple case or encoding tricks bypass literal matching regardless. Browsers don't universally block the tag, blocking one string doesn't break unrelated HTML, and XSS isn't limited to form submissions.
